questions.question: Kotlin class `Api` has `companion object { fun create(): Api = Api() }` with no annotations. How does Java code call it?
options: `Api.create()`
`Api.Companion.create()`
`new Api.Companion().create()`
`ApiKt.create()`
questions.explanation: A companion object compiles to a nested class `Api.Companion` with a static `Companion` field holding its single instance, so Java calls `Api.Companion.create()`. Adding `@JvmStatic` also generates a static `Api.create()` on the outer class. `ApiKt` is the facade class for top-level functions, not companion members.

questions.question: What happens to the lambda argument when you call a Kotlin `inline fun measure(block: () -> Unit)`?
options: It is compiled once into a shared singleton Function0 object that every call reuses
It is wrapped in a Runnable and executed synchronously on the calling thread
Both bodies are copied into the call site, so no Function object is created
It becomes an invokedynamic call site that is resolved and linked on first use
questions.explanation: Inlining copies both the function body and the lambda body into the caller, which removes the Function allocation and the virtual call and enables non-local `return`. Singleton Function objects and invokedynamic are how non-inline lambdas are compiled. The trade-off is bytecode size grows with every call site.

questions.question: Since Kotlin 2.0, non-inline lambdas compiled for the JVM use invokedynamic with LambdaMetafactory by default, instead of a generated class per lambda.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Kotlin 2.0 made invokedynamic generation of lambdas the default, matching how Java compiles lambdas and reducing the number of generated classes. On Android, D8 still processes these call sites when converting to dex, so the runtime shape may differ from plain JVM bytecode.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: true
false
It fails to compile because data classes cannot have body properties
It depends on the order the objects were created
questions.explanation: The generated `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy` and `componentN` only use properties declared in the primary constructor. `name` lives in the class body, so both objects compare equal on `id` alone. Body properties are allowed, which makes this a real source of cache and diffing bugs.

questions.question: This does not compile: the compiler reports an illegal usage of the inline parameter. Which change fixes it while keeping the function `inline`?
options: Mark the parameter `noinline`, so it is passed as a real Function object
Mark the parameter `crossinline`, so it is allowed to be saved into the field
Add a `reified` type parameter, so the lambda's type is kept around at runtime
Annotate `pending` with `@JvmField`, so the field can accept an inline lambda
questions.explanation: An inlined lambda has no object at runtime, so it cannot be assigned to a field. `noinline` makes that one parameter a normal Function instance. `crossinline` only forbids non-local returns so the lambda can be called from another execution context such as an object expression; it is still inlined and still cannot be stored directly.

questions.question: A release build sends `{"a":1,"b":"x"}` instead of `{"id":1,"name":"x"}` when serializing a model with Gson. Debug is fine. What is happening?
options: Gson switches to a compact field-naming policy when it detects a non-debuggable build
R8 merged the model class into another class, so Gson now reads the wrong fields
OkHttp's release logging interceptor minified the JSON body before sending it
R8 renamed the fields, and Gson takes JSON keys from field names via reflection
questions.explanation: Gson reads field names by reflection, and R8 obfuscation renamed them to short names in release. The fix is `@SerializedName` on the fields with matching keep rules, or keeping the model's fields, or moving to a codegen-based serializer like kotlinx.serialization. Gson has no build-type aware naming policy.

questions.question: With R8 enabled, which of these typically need you to write keep rules yourself? Select all that apply.
options: A Java method that native code looks up by name with `GetMethodID`
A sealed class used in an exhaustive `when` expression
An Activity that is declared in AndroidManifest.xml
A class instantiated via `Class.forName(prefix + name)` where the name is built at runtime
questions.explanation: R8 cannot see references made through runtime-built strings or from native code, so it may remove or rename those targets. Manifest components are kept by rules AAPT2 generates automatically. A `when` over a sealed class is an ordinary static reference that R8 traces like any other code.

questions.question: `-keepnames class com.app.Foo` stops R8 from renaming Foo, but R8 can still remove Foo entirely if nothing uses it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. `-keepnames` is shorthand for keep with `allowshrinking`, so it only protects the name of a class that survives shrinking. If you need the class to exist even when unreferenced, use `-keep`.

questions.question: A production crash shows `at a.b.c(Unknown Source:4)`. What do you need to turn it into readable class and method names?
options: The debug build's stack trace for the same crash, captured locally
The `mapping.txt` from that exact release build, used with retrace
The proguard-rules.pro file together with the app's current source code
A freshly rebuilt release APK from the current branch to compare against
questions.explanation: R8 writes `mapping.txt` for every minified build, and retrace (or the Play Console and crash tools when you upload it) maps obfuscated names back. The mapping must match that exact build; a rebuild from a later commit can produce different names. Keep rules alone do not describe how names were assigned.

questions.question: Which of these are optimizations R8 can perform on your app's bytecode? Select all that apply.
options: Converting `synchronized` blocks into lock-free code
Removing branches that constant propagation proves can never run
Merging a class into its only subclass or interface implementation
Inlining small methods into their callers
questions.explanation: R8's optimizer inlines methods, propagates constants and removes dead branches, and merges classes when the hierarchy allows it. These are also why stack traces can show fewer frames than the source suggests. It does not rewrite synchronization into lock-free algorithms; that would change semantics.
